displayQuote: No individual raindrop ever considers itself responsible for the flood

meta.title: Who really said "No individual raindrop ever considers itself responsible for the flood"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Douglas Adams. Quote Investigator traces it to columnist Sydney J. Harris, 2 March 1977. The Adams credit first appears in 2018, after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No individual raindrop ever considers itself responsible for the flood'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Douglas Adams — Quote Investigator’s earliest match is Sydney J. Harris’s syndicated column of 2 March 1977.

answer.label: Not Douglas Adams — actually Sydney J. Harris
answer.sourceLine: The earliest known printing is Sydney J. Harris’s syndicated column “Thoughts at large,” carried by the Tacoma News Tribune on 2 March 1977, where it runs as one of a string of unconnected one-line thoughts. Harris’s wording includes two words the internet has since dropped: “No individual raindrop ever considers itself to be responsible for the flood.” Quote Investigator found no substantive support for the Douglas Adams credit, which is not documented anywhere until 2018.

source.excerpt: No individual raindrop ever considers itself to be responsible for the flood.
trail: September 1963 — the idea reaches print in a different metaphor: “No snowflake in an avalanche ever feels responsible,” by Stanisław Jerzy Lec in Holiday magazine, translated by Jacek M. Galazka. Quote Investigator credits the snowflake form to Lec ↗.
2 March 1977 — the raindrop wording’s earliest documented appearance, in Sydney J. Harris’s “Thoughts at large” column in the Tacoma News Tribune. QI names Harris the leading candidate for creator ↗.

1979–1991 — the credit erodes. An article in Clinics in Plastic Surgery uses the line as an epigraph and names Harris in 1979; by 1980 a quotation compilation prints it with no author, and in May 1991 Forbes runs it as “ANONYMOUS.” All three citations are in QI’s chronology ↗.

2004 and 2018 — the famous names arrive. A Springville Herald page of filler items juxtaposes a Ruskin quotation with this one, and a Star Tribune column of 5 August 2018 gives a variant wording to Douglas Adams. QI documents both and supports neither ↗.
source.excerptNote: Harris’s column that day was a run of miscellaneous one-line thoughts on unrelated subjects — a note on a commonly misspelled word, a remark about what science calls natural laws — with the raindrop line sitting among them. There is no surrounding argument to quote: the sentence arrived already free-standing, which is part of why it detached so easily. Note the two extra words in the original: “considers itself to be responsible.” Nearly every modern reproduction drops them.

source.rightsHolder: Estate of Sydney J. Harris; column distributed by Field Newspaper Syndicate
source.rightsNote: The line was first published in a syndicated newspaper column on 2 March 1977, far too recent for the United States public domain — works first published in 1931 or later remain protected. Rights sit with Sydney J. Harris’s estate and with the successors to Field Newspaper Syndicate, which distributed the column. The single sentence is quoted here for identification and commentary; no public-domain status is claimed for it.

author.name: Sydney J. Harris
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote it
author.heading: Sydney J. Harris
author.metaLine: 1917–1986 · Chicago newspaper columnist, drama critic and essayist
author.bio: Born in London in 1917 and raised in the United States from the age of five, Sydney J. Harris started at the Chicago Herald and Examiner at seventeen and spent his career at the Chicago Daily News from 1944 until the paper folded in 1978, then at the Chicago Sun-Times until his death in 1986. His weekday column, “Strictly Personal,” ran in roughly 200 papers across the United States and Canada, and he published eleven books. His signature form was the compressed aphorism — a whole argument folded into one sentence — which is exactly the shape of the raindrop line, and exactly the shape that survives being cut loose from its author.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a saying with two famous claimants and a long stretch of no claimant at all. Neither famous name survives contact with the record.

items.why: Quote Investigator found no substantive support for the Adams credit. Its earliest documented instance is a Star Tribune weather column of 5 August 2018 — 41 years after Harris printed the line, and 17 years after Adams died in May 2001. Note also that the Adams credit attaches to a different wording: “The single raindrop never feels responsible for the flood.” That is the form the quote-aggregator sites reproduce under his name, not the sentence asked about here. The saying appears nowhere on Wikiquote’s Douglas Adams page.

QI records that on 30 September 2004 the Springville Herald of Springville, Utah ran two filler items in sequence: a quotation credited to John Ruskin, then this saying credited to “Anonymous.” QI notes it is possible an inattentive reader attached Ruskin’s name to the second item. The credit is still in circulation: The Gazette of Montreal ran it as Quote of the Day under Ruskin’s name on 23 April 2026.

E. C. McKenzie’s 1980 compilation Mac’s Giant Book of Quips & Quotes printed the line with no author named, and Forbes ran it on 27 May 1991 credited to “ANONYMOUS” — even though a 1979 article in Clinics in Plastic Surgery had used it as an epigraph and correctly credited Harris. Once the true author fell off, the slot was open.

misattribution.truthLine: On the evidence assembled by Quote Investigator, Sydney J. Harris wrote the line and published it in his syndicated column on 2 March 1977 — and a medical journal got the credit right two years later, before the rest of the world lost it.

context.heading: Why this one travels so well
lead: The saying works because it describes a real and uncomfortable thing: collective harm with no individually guilty party. Everyone in the crowd is a raindrop. Nobody in the crowd is the flood. It gets deployed on climate, on mob behaviour, on office culture, on traffic — anywhere responsibility dissolves the moment you divide it by the number of people involved.

That universality is also why it drifts. A line with no story attached — no scene, no book, no famous moment — is easy to move. It spent the 1980s and early 1990s in circulation as flatly anonymous: E. C. McKenzie’s 1980 compilation printed it with no author at all (and misspelled “responsible”), and Forbes ran it on 27 May 1991 credited only to “ANONYMOUS.” An unowned aphorism is a vacancy, and famous names get moved in to fill it.
detailsBody: The same idea reached print more than a decade before Harris, in a different metaphor. In September 1963 Holiday magazine printed a set of sayings by the Polish satirist Stanisław Jerzy Lec, translated by Jacek M. Galazka, including: “No snowflake in an avalanche ever feels responsible.”

Quote Investigator credits the snowflake saying to Lec on the strength of that 1963 citation, while noting that the original Polish wording has not yet been located. Whether Harris knew the snowflake version and re-cut it as rain, or arrived at the thought independently, is not something the record settles — and neither QI nor this page claims it does.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest match is Sydney J. Harris's syndicated column, Tacoma News Tribune, 2 March 1977, page A11 column 1, 'Thoughts at large' (Field Newspaper Syndicate), with the wording 'No individual raindrop ever considers itself to be responsible for the flood'; QI concludes Harris crafted the saying and found no substantive support for the John Ruskin or Douglas Adams attributions.

The same QI article documents the earliest Douglas Adams credit as the Star Tribune (Minneapolis), 5 August 2018, page B14, in the wording 'The single raindrop never feels responsible for the flood'; the 2004 Springville Herald juxtaposition that QI says may explain the Ruskin credit; the 1979 Clinics in Plastic Surgery epigraph crediting Harris; the 1980 McKenzie compilation with no author; the Forbes issue of 27 May 1991 crediting 'ANONYMOUS'; and The Gazette (Montreal) of 23 April 2026 still crediting Ruskin.

Quote Investigator credits 'No snowflake in an avalanche ever feels responsible' to Stanislaw Jerzy Lec on the basis of a September 1963 appearance in Holiday magazine translated by Jacek M. Galazka, and notes the original Polish statement has not yet been precisely located.
Quote Investigator's Douglas Adams tag page is QI's index of articles tagged Douglas Adams and includes the raindrop/flood investigation among seven listed articles.

Sydney J. Harris (14 September 1917, London – 7 December 1986, Chicago) was an American journalist for the Chicago Daily News and later the Chicago Sun-Times; he wrote 11 books and his weekday column 'Strictly Personal' was syndicated in roughly 200 newspapers in the US and Canada.

Wikiquote's Sydney J. Harris page collects sourced quotations organised under Strictly Personal (1953), On the Contrary (1964), The Best of Sydney J. Harris (1975), Pieces of Eight (1982) and Clearing the Ground (1986); the raindrop/flood saying does not appear on the page.

Wikiquote's Douglas Adams page contains no instance of the raindrop or flood saying, and its only top-level sections are Quotes, Quotes about Adams and External links — there is no Misattributed or Disputed section (verified against the raw wikitext, 38,328 bytes).
Douglas Adams was an English author, humourist and screenwriter who lived 11 March 1952 – 11 May 2001, dying in Santa Barbara, California.
The Internet Archive holds 'The Best of Sydney J. Harris', published by Houghton Mifflin in 1976, as an access-restricted lending item.
